item.content:encoded:
The regular season is rapidly coming to an end, and the Boston Red Sox still don't have ace pitcher Garrett Crochet back. That could be changing soon, though.
It had previously been reported that Crochet was set to return for the first round of the playoffs. Now, Chris Cotillo of MassLive noted in a report that the Red Sox may be pushing to have Crochet pitch in the regular season. This would act as a kind of rehab outing.
"The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason," Cotillo wrote. "It's not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what's effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings."
After finishing second in AL Cy Young voting in 2025, 2026 has been a major disappointment for Crochet. He has a 6.30 ERA and hasn't pitched since April 29th, when he originally hit the IL with left shoulder inflammation. He would later also be diagnosed with a lat strain.
When Crochet does return, it won't be in the rotation. He doesn't have time to build up to that. Instead, the Red Sox are going to be using him out of the bullpen. he
Boston Red Sox Ace Garrett Crochet Doesn't Have Time for a Rehab
The reality for Garrett Crochet is that time is running out for a rehab assignment, and he likely won't have time to make one. That's why the Red Sox would likely want to bring him back before a playoff series.
Regardless of if that chance to come back before the postseason happens, however, Crochet is confident in himself.
"Someone brought it up the other day. They were like, isn't that crazy? I'm like, not really," Crochet said on Monday. "I mean, not [to be all] me, me, me, me, but I've done crazy things before. I'm not Joe Schmoe. I've done impressive things. I think that that would be a big ask for some people, but I don't think it's a crazy ask for me."
This isn't entirely new territory for Crochet. In 2020, the Chicago White Sox added him to their postseason roster when he had limited time in live action due to the pandemic and coming out of college. He pitched well in that brief opportunity, throwing 0.2 innings with 2 strikeouts.
The Red Sox Postseason Rotation is Up for Debate
Heading into the postseason, pitching is a strength for the Red Sox. Even with injuries, that much has become obvious. Still, questions remain about the actual rotation in the postseason.
Sonny Gray and Payton Tolle will make starts in a three-game series. That's not up for debate. There is debate about which of the two gets Game One. Then, Game Three is going to be between Ranger Suarez and Jake Bennett. The lean there is certainly for the well-paid Suarez, who is a veteran with postseason success. However, stranger things have happened.
Starters who could be coming back from injury, including Houck and Crochet, are going to be seen as relievers. That's presumably how the Red Sox will also continue to use Brayan Bello and Patrick Sandoval.

item.content:encoded:
Alex Cora said Braiden Ward would be a factor in October.
The Boston Red Sox outfield depth took a major hit ahead of last Friday’s series opener against the Kansas City Royals as the team placed Eli White on the 10-day injured list with a right foot ligament injury, with no timetable for his return. The 32-year-old outfielder not only filled in admirably for the injured Ceddanne Rafaela, but was also slated to play an important role on the postseason roster as the fourth outfielder and pinch runner off the bench. With White now unlikely to return before the postseason, could the Red Sox turn to spring-training standout Braiden Ward to fill the role?
About Ward
The Red Sox acquired Ward in an offseason deal with the Colorado Rockies in exchange for left-handed reliever Brennan Bernardino. The 27-year-old outfielder became one of the biggest storylines of Red Sox spring training, seeing ample playing time as many of Boston's outfield options, including Roman Anthony, Wilyer Abreu and Rafaela, represented their countries in the World Baseball Classic. In 27 Grapefruit League games, Ward hit .378/.509/.444/.953 while stealing 19 bases, setting a single-season spring training record. Ward's dynamic speed caught the eye of now-former manager Alex Cora, who told reporters on several occasions that the 27-year-old would be a factor come October.
After missing the team's opening-day roster amid an already crowded outfield, Ward spent the entire 2026 season in Triple-A Worcester. In 107 games with the WooSox, Ward hit just .238/.356/.355/.711 but set a record for most stolen bases in a single season for a Red Sox Triple-A club with 58 and counting.
There's just one problem...
While Ward seems like a slam-dunk option to fill White's role on the postseason roster, it is not as simple as just recalling him from Triple-A, as he's not on the 40-man roster. The Red Sox 40-man roster currently sits at 39; however, the impending returns of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo mean the team will have to either designate two players for assignment or move someone to the 60-day IL.
Luckily, there are several candidates for the latter: in White, should he be unable to return for the postseason, designated hitter Masataka Yoshida, utility man Anthony Seigler and reliever Justin Slaten, all of whom appear unlikely to return prior to the end of the season.
Is Ward actually an option?
Interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league club during his weekly appearance on WEEI's 'Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson' Show on Wednesday afternoon. "I think that'd be considered for sure," he said when asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league team. "It's really hard to predict what a roster could look like, but you definitely can't ignore a 60-stolen-base player," he continued.
However, Tracy cautioned that a pinch runner is a last resort for a team when it's trailing, and teams must consider other options, like whether it would be more valuable to add another right-handed bat or a better defender to the roster. Though Ward does profile as an above-average outfield defender.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener, the Red Sox will look to even up the three-game set with the Texas Rangers in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON -- Tanner Houck continued his rehab assignment with his third Minor League appearance on Tuesday, while Garrett Crochet threw another bullpen session at Fenway Park as both worked toward returning to Boston in relief roles.
The right-hander entered in the seventh and struck out Oliver Dunn looking at a 94.1 mph fastball. He then walked a batter before getting Austin Slater to swing through a 93.6 mph four-seamer and Jack Suwinski to chase an 83.5 mph sweeper.
Houck threw 22 pitches (11 strikes) and reached 94.2 mph with his fastball.
The 30-year-old is expected to make his next appearance on Friday, when he is scheduled for a longer outing in the 45-, 50-pitch range.
“Obviously some swing and miss in there. He has that capability,” interim manager Chad Tracy said ahead of Boston's bout with the Rangers Wednesday. “We all know -- and he said [it] himself, each time he touches the mound, getting his rhythm -- he gets a little bit more comfortable. That's all part of it. The strike-throwing piece and getting command of your pitches.
“So it seems at this point he's at least taking a step forward each time he goes out there, which is good. This next one will be good, being able to see [if he can] replicate that over a longer stretch of pitches.”
Crochet also took another step in his recovery.
The 2025 American League Cy Young Award runner-up threw a 30-pitch bullpen session at Fenway Park. Tracy said the session went well, but as of Wednesday the team did not have much clarity on Crochet’s next steps. He will continue his throwing program this week before the Red Sox re-evaluate him over the weekend.
Crochet has been building up his workload and intensity in recent bullpen sessions. He threw 25 pitches in his previous session Friday, when he incorporated his sweeper and threw his fastball in the 92-93 mph range.

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are anticipating some major additions for the postseason, from the long-awaited returns of Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck to the expected activation of Ceddanne Rafaela. A prospect who has yet to debut in the majors could be nearly as impactful.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy hinted Wednesday that speedster Braiden Ward could be called up with the postseason looming, after a dominant season on the basepaths in the minor leagues.
Ward, who would have to be added to the 40-man roster, would be eligible for the postseason despite spending the entire year in triple-A Worcester up to this point.
Here's more to know about Ward and his potential call-up.
Who is Braiden Ward?
Tracy told WEEI's "Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson" that Ward could be called up at some point soon. "I think that would be considered, for sure," Tracy said.
Chad Tracy on @richkented talking about potentially calling up Braiden Ward: 'I think that would be considered, for sure.'
— Rob Bradford (@bradfo) September 16, 2026
Ward is 27, which is older than a typical prospect, but he would be coming up for something that can't necessarily be taught: speed. A 16th-round pick out of Washington in 2021, Ward leads triple-A with 58 stolen bases this season and has 269 career minor-league stolen bases in 519 games.
Originally drafted by the Rockies, Ward spent four years in Colorado's system before coming over in return for reliever Brennan Bernardino in a November trade last year.
Pinch-runners can be valuable in the postseason if there is room on the roster, and a foot injury for Eli White could play a role in opening up some space for Ward even if his bat isn't much of a tool the Red Sox can use in October.
Here's a full look at Ward's minor-league stats in 2026.
Braiden Ward Minor League Stats
| Games | AVG | HR | RBI | H | SB | OPS |
| 105 | .238 | 5 | 29 | 87 | 58 | .712 |
Ward hasn't had a strong season offensively, batting .238 without flashing much power, but he still gets on base at more than a 35 percent clip and has a career .386 minor-league on base percentage in part because he has a penchant for getting hit by pitches; Ward has been hit 30 times in 2026.
If the Red Sox give Ward a chance down the stretch, it will be because of his speed. Ward's 58 stolen bases are the most in either triple-A league, and a bit of additional speed on the basepaths in the postseason, when games tend to be lower-scoring, could make a major difference for Boston.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox could have a slew of pitching reinforcements returning before the playoffs begin, including Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, and maybe even Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Justin Slaten will not be among them.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on September 15 told reporters (including Tim Healey of The Boston Globe) that Slaten got a PRP injection in his arm to address a flexor issue. His season is over after multiple attempts to ramp up for a rehab assignment and eventual return.
Slaten has been quite injury prone over his three years with the Red Sox. He went on the injured list for the first time this season in early April and didn't return until mid-May. For the second straight year, he'll finish his season with less than 35 innings pitched.
Justin Slaten's season with Red Sox ends after he gets PCP injection for flexor injury
The righty has dabbled in the extremes this season, finishing with a 4.60 ERA over 31.1 innings. In June, Slaten's worst month this year, he allowed nine runs on 17 hits over 11 outings. July was his best, during which he let up just one run on five hits over nine appearances. His WHIP has starkly increased over the past year, from 1.09 in 2025 to 1.37.
When the Red Sox can get Slaten's best, he's one of the biggest threats out of their bullpen. But he's often injured or prone to blowups that keep him from showing the best he can offer. It will be interesting to see his role next season when Boston has more healthy pitching depth it could push to the bullpen.
Red Sox confirm Kristian Campbell's season is over due to foot injury, ending breakout
Kristian Campbell's season has also ended prematurely due to an injury. The outfielder will be out for the rest of the year due to a left foot contusion, according to Tommy Cassell of the Worcester Telegram & Gazette.
The WooSox pulled Campbell from their September 8 game due to the injury. Even before the announcement of his IL stint, it was evident that Campbell's season could be over, as Worcester's last regular season game is on Septembet 20.
Campbell's injury ends a resurgent second half for the 24 year old. He slashed .311/.430/.497 over 51 games after the All-Star break and, had he been healthy, he might've been selected to come up and help the major league team while Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White are injured.
Romy Gonzalez continues tear following arm injury scare with WooSox
On the same day Campbell was pulled from the WooSox's lineup, Romy Gonzalez was, too. An arm injury led to a week on the shelf for the utility infielder, but he joined the Triple-A lineup again on September 15.
Gonzalez has resumed the tear he was on before his arm flared up. He logged two hits, including a double, in his return and boosted his September slash line to .500/.520/.727 over six games. Gonzalez has hit so well lately that it could be time to call him back up to the major leagues to give Boston's slumping offense a boost.

item.content:encoded:
The WooSox roster has a bunch of guys who’ve made some plays for the Major League roster this season. But, as far as the Triple-A club is concerned, few guys (I know, I know, Franklin Arias might be one) have had as many big moments as Allan Castro. This wasn’t the 23-year-old’s strongest season from an OPS standpoint, but the big moments are getting notable. He just had a go-ahead home run the other day and he’s had multiple other walkoffs throughout the season. Yesterday, the WooSox again started a series on the winning side due to his bat, as he hit a 2-out single to score the Manfred runner. And, yes, in the process of all of this, Franklin Arias got himself a knock as did Romy Gonzalez. (Here’s that Castro hit.)
The game in general was a defensive battle. The Durham Bulls (Rays AAA) had the benefit of up-and-down starter Mason Englart dealing on Tuesday night as they couldn’t get on the board until Englart departed after seven. Luckily, Jedixson Paez was just as hot even without some of the strikeout numbers. His only run allowed was via a home run way back on the second at-bat of the game, and the 22-year-old righty recovered wonderfully from that, retiring fifteen consecutive Durham batters. From there, Tanner Houck came in and struck out the side in his rehab appearance, and it is starting to look likely that he sees some innings in a relief capacity as the Red Sox’s magic number dwindles. Osvaldo Berrios and Hobie Harris would then slam the door even in the face of a few more Bulls scoring opportunities; the WooSox had the only opportunity with runners in scoring position of the game. Enter extra innings, and enter Castro’s sealing single. Game over, 2-1.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Justin Slaten's Injury Costs Red Sox Dearly With Playoffs Looming
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
Over the last few weeks, or so, it has seemed like pretty much every injury update for the Boston Red Sox has been positive.
Garrett Crochet has been throwing, Tanner Houck has been on a rehab assignment and even Curtis Mead has been playing catch, among others. While this is the case, the Red Sox gave a negative update on Wednesday. Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy shared that reliever Justin Slaten is dealing with "degenerative changes in the flexor mass" and is likely done for the 2026 season.
"Slaten, we got ... he went and saw [Dr. Keith Meister] with our medical staff today and there's some degenerative changes in the flexor mass," Tracy said. "So he's going to be down. He's going to get a PRP injection and it's likely going to end his season. So, that's substantially different news, as far as these guys."
Bad News For Boston
This is a brutal blow for Slaten, and the Red Sox's bullpen in general. Slaten is one of the club's key high-leverage guys, but Boston hasn't had him on the mound since Aug. 12. He was initially placed on the Injured List due to right elbow inflammation. He actually started throwing, but he had to be shut down when the same "symptoms" that landed him on the Injured List popped up again.
Slaten had a 4.60 ERA in 36 appearances, but this doesn't tell the full story about why he's a big loss for Boston. In his final 17 appearances of the season, he had a 2.45 ERA and a 19-to-3 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 14 2/3 innings pitched. The first half of the season wasn't great for him, but he had turned things around and looked like the guy Boston hoped it would have out of the bullpen.
The Red Sox have just 11 games left in the 2026 regular season. Losing Slaten hurts Boston's playoff chances. On the bright side, the Red Sox's bullpen could still get better with Houck on a minor league rehab assignment and Garrett Crochet throwing as well. With Slaten likely out for the season, that's one less change Boston will have to make when building the playoff roster. Tyron Guerrero, Crochet, and Houck are all inching their way back. Boston will have to clear three spots to get these guys on the roster. That could be bad news for guys like Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, and Raymond Burgos, among others.
With Slaten likely not coming back, it's one less decision for Boston to make. Of course, it would be better if he were returning, but that isn't the case right now. Unfortunately, Red Sox fans have seemingly seen the last of Slaten for the 2026 season.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Patrick Sandoval allows four runs in second, Red Sox lose opener to Rangers
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second. item.content:encoded:
Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. Entering Tuesday, the Red Sox left-hander had allowed a 6.12 ERA over his last five starts, but coming out of the gate Sandoval looked like he’d finally figured things out.
But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second.
Sandoval allowed four runs over an interminable 44-pitch second inning and ultimately got the hook after recording just eight outs in Boston’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers.
Nick Sogard hit a two-run home run to help get the Red Sox back into the game, but the offense otherwise couldn’t get anything going against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers bullpen, squandering bases loaded opportunities in the fifth and eighth innings.
Sandoval started strong by striking out the side in the first inning, but after sending down Jake Burger to start the second everything ground to a screeching halt. The right-hander allowed a pair of singles, served up a two-run double to Elias Diaz, and then walked back-to-back batters to load the bases for five-time All-Star Corey Seager.
It appeared for a moment like Sandoval might minimize the damage when he drew a pop fly to shallow left, but the ball drifted into no-man’s land and Trevor Story couldn’t make the catch, allowing two more runs to score and putting the Rangers up 4-0.
Sandoval ultimately needed 44 pitches to get through the second, blowing up his pitch count and ensuring a long evening for the Red Sox bullpen. He recorded two outs in the third and was lifted for Brayan Bello after allowing four runs over 2 2/3 innings.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Arlington postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
Four runs matches the largest deficit the Red Sox have overcome in a win this season, but the club didn’t need long to cut it in half. After Caleb Durbin reached on a one-out single in the top of the third, Sogard ripped a line drive off deGrom that cleared the right field fence for a two-run home run.
It was the fifth home run of the season for Sogard, all of which have come since Aug. 19. Prior to that the 29-year-old had never hit a homer over his first three seasons as a big leaguer.
That wound up being as close as Boston got.
The Red Sox could have tied the score or taken the lead with one swing in the fifth inning, but despite loading the bases without recording a hit the club couldn’t get a run across. Jarren Duran was hit by a pitch, Durbin reached on catcher’s interference and Mickey Gasper walked to bring up Adley Rutschman with two outs, but the catcher grounded out to short to keep it a 4-2 game.
Boston’s bullpen did its part to keep the Red Sox in the game. Bello tossed 1 2/3 perfect innings, Alec Gamboa threw one scoreless aided in large part by a brilliant double play turned by Sogard to end the fifth, and Wyatt Olds worked his way out of a runners-at-the-corners, two-out jam to escape the sixth. Jovani Moran entered with a man on in the seventh and got three quick outs, setting the table for one last Red Sox push in the eighth.
Jahmai Jones sparked the rally with a leadoff single, Willson Contreras drew a one-out walk, and after Wilyer Abreu grounded out to move the two runners into scoring position Story was intentionally walked to load the bases again.
Rather than have Duran face the left-hander Jacob Latz, Tracy pinch hit Andruw Monasterio, but the move didn’t pay off. Monasterio worked a full count and nearly went deep on a hard hit liner that landed just foul before striking out to leave them loaded again.
Boston went quietly in the top of the ninth, finishing the game 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position while stranding nine men on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up and we couldn’t do it tonight,” Tracy said.
Magic number still 5
In addition to keeping pace in the AL West race, the Rangers also jumped the Toronto Blue Jays to become the first team below the AL Wild Card cutline. As a result the Red Sox’s magic number remains five despite the Blue Jays’ 10-1 loss earlier in the night.
Boston (82-69) can clinch a playoff berth as early as Friday, and depending on how things play out in the AL Central the Red Sox could lock down the second Wild Card spot as soon as this weekend.
Houck scoreless with WooSox
Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery rehab) tossed a scoreless inning of relief in his latest rehab appearance with the WooSox on Tuesday. The right-hander entered the game in the seventh inning and allowed one walk, no hits and struck out three over 22 pitches.

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 season has been, for the most part, an injury-plagued loss for Crochet, who made his first six starts before getting shut down with left shoulder inflammation that regressed when he made his first attempted comeback in late May.
But the beauty of all this is that Crochet can wash away the sour taste of missing most of the season by getting back as a reliever in time for the most important games.
After that setback at the end of May, it took Crochet three months just to be cleared to throw off the mound again.
Now that he’s been able to do so three times, and is scheduled for a fourth bullpen session at Fenway Park on Tuesday, there is legitimate hope he can be on the roster when the Red Sox open their postseason on Sept. 29 -- likely at Yankee Stadium.
This time, assuming he makes it back, Crochet will be cast in a much different role, but one that can still be impactful.
Figuring you have questions about how and when Crochet fits in, here are some answers.
Can Crochet make it back before the regular season ends?
It’s not impossible. His next key step after graduating from bullpen sessions will be to face hitters. That could happen as soon as this weekend, depending on what the club decides after Tuesday’s session.
Ideally, when it comes to Crochet’s situation, the Triple-A season would go a little longer. But, alas, it ends on Sunday.
It seems more likely Crochet will throw live batting practice and/or some type of simulated game rather than getting into a Minor League game, perhaps doing so multiple times.
Would this leave time for one tune-up before the regular season ends on Sept. 27? Perhaps, but not necessarily.
Would Crochet be thrown right into the fire of the playoffs?
What if there isn’t time for Crochet to pitch in any type of game setting before the Wild Card Series starts? Would the Red Sox still put him on the roster?
Well, if he’s throwing up to his capabilities, the answer is absolutely yes.
“It's Garrett Crochet,” said Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “If Garrett Crochet looks like Garrett Crochet and he's healthy and able to go out there and pitch, and it looks like him? Yeah, that helps any team.”
What would Boston’s bullpen cast look like with Crochet in the mix?
In a word, dominant. Through their first 150 games of the season entering Tuesday, Boston’s bullpen has a 3.11 ERA, best in the Majors. That’s without Crochet.
Now, add Crochet and possibly 2024 Tanner Houck, who is on a Minor League rehab assignment in his return from Tommy John surgery, and Tracy’s relief crew could have a succession of pitchers with nasty stuff.
At 38 years old, lefty Aroldis Chapman continues to be a force. He has one of the best eighth-inning setup men in the game in front of him in righty Garrett Whitlock. Tyron Guerrero, the righty with triple-digit heat, is due back in the next couple of days after missing the last couple of weeks with right shoulder inflammation. Power lefty Erik Miller has been tremendous since he was acquired at the Aug. 3 Trade Deadline.
Brayan Bello, who hasn’t had much success has a starter this season but has been largely stellar in relief, is another weapon. Add Crochet and Houck to those five pitchers and the Sox would have bullpen depth that would be the envy of most teams.
How would the Sox use Crochet?
The beauty of Crochet is that he could work out of a hybrid role, meaning he could be available for whichever part of the game Tracy needs him most.
Keep in mind that Crochet was a relief pitcher not just in college at Tennessee, but also for the White Sox before being converted to a starting role in ‘24. He has experience working in the early, middle and late part of games.
Thinking outside the box, the Sox could even deploy Crochet as an opener if the occasion called for it, given his experience starting games.
“He'd have plenty of comfort opening if you wanted to go that route," Tracy said. "He pitched out of the 'pen. So if you need him to come in the middle innings of a game, a two-inning pocket, I'm sure he'd have comfort doing that, too."

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox fans will not be seeing former top prospect Kristian Campbell in the big leagues at all this season, unfortunately.
On Tuesday, Tommy Cassell of the Worcester T&G Sports reported that Campbell's season is over. Campbell was placed on the seven-day Injured List due to a left foot contusion on Sep. 10. Cassell reported that Campbell will not be able to return before Triple-A Worcester's season ends on Sep. 20.
"Some injury updates today in AAA Worcester: Tanner Houck is scheduled to pitch one inning (20-25 pitches) in relief," Cassell wrote. "Romy Gonzalez is in at DH despite being a bit banged up. Iggy Suarez mentioned he's "an option" to contribute with the Red Sox moving forward. Kristian Campbell is out for the rest of the WooSox season. 'He was a big part of what we've been doing,' Suarez said. 'So, it's definitely a downer for that.'"
Kristian Campbell Is Done For The Year
That's some really unfortunate news for one of the most intriguing players in the Red Sox's system. Campbell made the big league club out of Spring Training in 2025 as the first member of the "Big 3," including him, Roman Anthony and Marcelo Mayer. He was red-hot out of the gate to the point that Boston handed him an eight-year, $60 million deal. But things took a turn afterward. Campbell was demoted to Triple-A in June, 2025. He hasn't been in the majors since.
Campbell played in 73 down in Triple-A last season and then didn't make the Red Sox's big league club out of camp. He has been down in the minors all season this year trying to work his way back.
The 24-year-old spent the season in the outfield as Boston tried to slow things down after moving him around all over the place last year. For Boston, it is loaded in the outfield to the point that there was a logjam early on in the season. Then, despite the Red Sox losing Roman Anthony to the Injured List for a while, there still wasn't space for Campbell in the majors.
Overall, Campbell wrapped up his season after playing in 109 games for Triple-A and slashing .256/.383/.380 with a .763 OPS, eight homers and 51 RBIs. Hopefully, he's able to get back on track and get back into the mix by the time Spring Training rolls around. Who could've seen this coming back in 2025? Campbell looked like a franchise cornerstone piece. Unfortunately, he hasn't been in the majors in over a year and now that won't be happening this year.

item.content:encoded:
Over the last few weeks, the Boston Red Sox have gotten positive updates left and right about injured starting pitchers.
First and foremost, Garrett Crochet has been throwing and is trending towards a late-season return in Boston's bullpen, barring a setback. Tanner Houck has been on a minor league rehab assignment and is trending up. Plus, the current expectation is that Johan Oviedo is nearing a minor league rehab assignment as well. Now, it sounds like another hurler is trending up as well. On Tuesday, Tommy Cassell of the Worcester T&G Sports reported that there have been "some rumblings" that Kutter Crawford could join Triple-A Worcester throughout the week as well.
"And there are some rumblings that Kutter Crawford could be in Worcester this week, too," Cassell wrote. "The 30-year-old righty has been sidelined since March with right wrist and forearm issues and made one rehab stint with Worcester on April 11 before being shut down again. Crawford hasn’t been confirmed yet whether he will pitch in Worcester."
Kutter Crawford Is Trending Up
How about that?
Crawford hasn't been talked about in a long time. Now, it seems like the righty could potentially be in Worcester this week. Things move quickly in baseball, to say the least.
Crawford missed the entire 2025 season and he was trending up at one point early in the 2026 season and even went on a rehab assignment with Triple-A Worcester, although he suffered a setback and has been on the shelf ever since.
Now, of course, this doesn't guarantee that he will help the Red Sox before the 2026 season comes to a close. In fact, it arguably would be surprising to see him on the Red Sox's roster before the season comes to a close. Crawford's last appearance in a game was on April 11, 2026 with Worcester. When he does take the mound again, he's going to have to build up and get the rust off. The regular season will end for the Red Sox in just 12 days, as of writing, on Sep. 27. That's not a lot of time to begin a rehab assignment for the first time in five months and return to the majors with the playoffs looming.
But it's still good news in general for Boston. What if Crawford does pitch this week for Triple-A Worcester and looks like a game-changer? Maybe, he could surprise. Even if he doesn't, he's under team control for the 2027 and 2028 seasons. If the Red Sox could enter Spring Training with Crawford as a legit candidte for either the rotation — or even the bullpen — that makes the team better. Or, if he proves he's healthy, maybe he could even be an intriguing trade chip this winter.
All in all, hearing that one of the Red Sox's hurlers are trending up after missing so much time is positive in itself.

item.content:encoded:
Being the longest-tenured pitcher on the Red Sox staff has been a lonely role for Garrett Whitlock this year, and one he is eager to hand back to its rightful owner.
The right-hander has been elite in his sixth big-league season, all with Boston. Whitlock entered Monday’s off-day with a 1.81 ERA, 31.2 strikeout percentage and 3.8 walk percentage, all career bests, through 51 appearances, with 58 strikeouts and just seven walks in 49 2/3 innings.
On Monday, Whitlock was announced as the Red Sox nominee for Major League Baseball’s prestigious Roberto Clemente Award, “bestowed annually to the player who best represents the game of baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions, both on and off the field.”
But Whitlock has spent most of his excellent campaign without his closest friend on the team: fellow righty Tanner Houck, who spent most of the season down at the club’s Fort Myers, Fla., spring training complex, rehabbing from his August 2025 Tommy John surgery.
Which meant that for the first time in half a decade, Whitlock and Houck celebrated their June birthdays – they each turned 30 on the 11th and 29th, respectively – apart. They typically play card or board games, cribbage and euchre are among their favorites, and get ice cream with their wives.
“We always do something to celebrate, hang out at each other’s apartments or houses, and everything,” Whitlock told the Herald. “So it was weird not having that this year. And so yeah, it’s nice to have my best friend back.”
Houck finally returned to Boston at the start of the last homestand, then began a rehab assignment in the minor leagues. He is on track to rejoin the Red Sox for the tail-end of the regular season, and for what they hope will be the team’s first deep playoff run since 2021, when he and Whitlock were the rookies of the pitching staff.
“So good to have him back,” Whitlock said. “Love seeing him in the locker room, and the guys love having him around. So excited for him to get back with us soon.”
Whitlock is eager to return the title of longest-tenured Red Sox player to Houck when he returns to the active roster. Tuesday marks the six-year anniversary of Houck’s MLB debut. Whitlock arrived several months later via the Rule 5 Draft, and debuted at the start of the 2021 season. Together, the two righties have ridden the highest of highs and lowest of lows in the years since: a stunningly successful 2021 season, their respective season-ending surgeries in 2022, Whitlock’s season-ending elbow surgery in May 2024, and Houck’s last summer. Houck supported Whitlock through the sudden death of his younger brother, Gavrie, in 2023, and celebrated when Whitlock became a father in the summer of 2024.
“It’s huge,” Whitlock said of his relationship with Houck. “Everyone’s left, and we’re still here. … We’ve been through everything together, through all the changes, whether it’s front office changes, coaching staff changes, our health changes, literally everything.
“It’s been one of those things that we’ve been through so much together that just grows your friendship, and so it’s nice to have a familiar face back around, and my best friend on the team, and I’m looking forward to sharing the rest of the year with him.”
The Red Sox plan to use Houck in a relief role, which will put him and Whitlock in the bullpen together for the first time since 2022.
“He’s got elite stuff,” Whitlock said. “You saw when he was the closer in ‘22, how good his stuff is. And so I’m excited for – I think people were writing him off before he had surgery, and I’m excited for people to see Tanner be Tanner again. And I think as soon as he shows that, people will start coming back and loving him again, and it’ll be great to have that.”
Whitlock and Houck are the only active pitchers in the organization who know what it’s like to play a postseason home game at Fenway Park. (Boston’s lone playoff appearance since was last year’s three-game wild card series, all of which played out at Yankee Stadium.)
“It was a crazy ride,” Whitlock recalled of 2021. “The whole thing was surreal, because rookie year, I never even expected to be there. So it was surreal, and loved every second of it, and want some more. We’re ready to get back.”
Though some may scoff at the importance of such experience, many Red Sox players and opponents know that October at Fenway is a whole other animal. Whitlock, and, he hopes, Houck are looking forward to sharing their experience with younger teammates.
“I think the biggest thing I will tell them is, don’t change what’s gotten you here,” Whitlock said. “So many times, people try and do so many different things, in the playoffs and pressure situations, and it’s like, you can’t do that.
“You’ve got to do exactly what brought you to these moments, because it worked. It worked to get you there. It worked to get you to these moments, and so you can’t try and do more. You can’t try and change anything. Keep doing exactly what you’ve been doing, because what got you here is good enough to get you through it.”
But first, the Red Sox must punch their ticket. They entered Monday’s off-day with their magic number down to six.
“Those conversations haven’t really started just quite yet, because it’s like, alright, we still got some work to do to get to the playoffs,” Whitlock said. “Hopefully the closer we get, those will start picking up.
“But I’m excited. We’re at the door, so we just need to finish our job, and get in.”

item.content:encoded:
Tanner Houck started his career with plenty of hype, acting as someone who can do anything if given the opportunity. Coming off an injury that kept him out of action throughout he 2026 season, he hopes the Red Sox could use him come playoff time.
The 24th overall pick in the 2017 MLB Draft, Houck was picked up as a starting pitcher. A chameleon, he adapted to any situation, acting as a starter, reliever, and closer. In 2022, he appeared in 32 games and was as durable as one could be.
Houck has shown flashes of brilliance but hasn’t found consistency. This year, he has been rehabbing after undergoing a special surgery of his ulnar collateral ligament. It’s a "hybrid reconstruction" with a flexor tendon repair.
That was last August. This year, the Red Sox, with high expectations, struggled at first. Now, they are playoff contenders, and Houck wouldn’t mind adding to the fun. That includes rejoining the team before the season ended.
"I had my mind set on one goal, going out there and just helping this team this year," Houck said via The Boston Globe. "I just truly believed that I could do it."
The recovery process was expected to be 12-14 months. However, Houck recently appeared in minor league rehab game and is scheduled to pitch for Triple-A Worcester on Tuesday and Saturday. His determination to compete comes at an interesting time.
As of September 14, the Red Sox are 8.5 games behind the Rays in the AL East. They own the second Wild Card spot with just a few weeks to go in the regular season. Catching the Yankees, on top of the Wild Card, would be ideal.
Houck is one of a few Red Sox members to experience playoff baseball at Fenway Park. If he’s cleared, it doesn’t matter the role given, Houck hopes he can just make a difference.
"Three innings out of the pen is a little bit more appealing than just being a one-inning limited-pitch-count guy," Houck said. "So if I can get built up for 40-50 pitches and help out in any way, then it’s a lot easier role. Any role that I can step in and go out there and help this team win, I’m in."

item.content:encoded:
We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.
